stimuli.title: Two rows facing south, one behind the other
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Aalok, Binita, Chakshu, Dhanvi, Ehsaan, Fenil, Gauransh and Hetal sit in two rows of four seats each. Everyone faces south. Row 1 is the front row; Row 2 is directly behind it, so each person in Row 2 sits directly behind one person in Row 1. (Facing south, the right is towards the west and the left towards the east.)

- Aalok sits in the front row, second from the right end of that row.
- Gauransh sits directly behind Aalok, and Chakshu sits immediately to the left of Gauransh.
- Dhanvi sits second to the left of Aalok, and Ehsaan sits directly behind Dhanvi.
- Hetal sits in the front row at one of its ends.
- Binita does not sit in the front row.
stimuli.solution:
Number the columns 1 to 4 from the west. Facing south, the right end of a row is its west end.
Step 1: Aalok = Row 1, column 2. Gauransh = Row 2, column 2; Chakshu, to his left (east): Row 2, column 3.
Step 2: Dhanvi is second to Aalok's left: Row 1, column 4; Ehsaan behind her: Row 2, column 4.
Step 3: Free seats: Row 1 columns 1 and 3, Row 2 column 1. Hetal is at an end of the front row: column 1. Binita is not in the front row: Row 2, column 1. Fenil = Row 1, column 3.

| Column (from west) | Row 1 (front) | Row 2 (behind) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hetal | Binita |
| 2 | Aalok | Gauransh |
| 3 | Fenil | Chakshu |
| 4 | Dhanvi | Ehsaan |

stimuli.title: Seven players in a row, with jersey numbers
stimuli.content:
Seven players Kuldeep, Lipsa, Murari, Nandan, Paridhi, Ruchika and Somnath sit in a straight row, all facing north. Their jersey numbers are 7, 9, 10, 14, 18, 21 and 23, a different number for each player. (Facing north, the right is towards the east.)

- Lipsa sits exactly in the middle of the row and wears the smallest number.
- The person wearing 23 sits at the extreme left end of the row.
- Kuldeep sits immediately to the right of Lipsa, and his number is twice Murari's.
- Nandan sits at the extreme right end, and his number is three times Lipsa's.
- Ruchika sits immediately to the left of Nandan, and Somnath sits second to the left of Kuldeep.
- Murari does not sit at an end of the row.
- Somnath's number is greater than Ruchika's.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 7 from the left.
Step 1: Lipsa = 4 (number 7). Kuldeep = 5, Nandan = 7 with 3 × 7 = 21, Ruchika = 6, Somnath = 3.
Step 2: Seats 1 and 2 remain for Murari and Paridhi; Murari is not at an end: Murari = 2, Paridhi = 1. The number 23 is at the left end: Paridhi.
Step 3: 9, 10, 14 and 18 remain for Murari, Somnath, Kuldeep and Ruchika. Kuldeep = 2 × Murari: 18 and 9. Somnath's number is greater than Ruchika's: Somnath 14, Ruchika 10.

| Seat | Player | Number |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Paridhi | 23 |
| 2 | Murari | 9 |
| 3 | Somnath | 14 |
| 4 | Lipsa | 7 |
| 5 | Kuldeep | 18 |
| 6 | Ruchika | 10 |
| 7 | Nandan | 21 |

stimuli.title: Six persons around a round table, with coloured caps
stimuli.content:
Six persons Daya, Kirpal, Nutan, Pinki, Ramesh and Sonu sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. Each wears a cap of a different colour among Black, Green, Orange, Red, White and Yellow. (Facing the centre, a person's right is anticlockwise and the left clockwise.)

- Kirpal sits opposite Daya, and Sonu sits immediately to the left of Kirpal.
- Nutan sits immediately between Daya and Sonu.
- Pinki sits immediately to the left of Daya.
- Daya wears the Red cap, and the person wearing the Green cap sits opposite her.
- The person wearing the White cap sits immediately to the right of Daya.
- The person wearing the Black cap sits second to the left of Ramesh.
- Pinki does not wear the Yellow cap.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 5 anticlockwise from Daya.
Step 1: Kirpal = 3 (opposite). Sonu, to Kirpal's left (clockwise): 2. Nutan sits between Daya and Sonu: 1. Pinki, to Daya's left: 5. Ramesh = 4.
Step 2: Daya Red, Kirpal (opposite) Green, Nutan (Daya's right) White. Black is second to Ramesh's left (clockwise from 4): seat 2, Sonu.
Step 3: Orange and Yellow remain for Ramesh and Pinki; Pinki does not wear Yellow: Pinki Orange, Ramesh Yellow.

| Seat (anticlockwise) | Person | Cap |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Daya | Red |
| 1 | Nutan | White |
| 2 | Sonu | Black |
| 3 | Kirpal | Green |
| 4 | Ramesh | Yellow |
| 5 | Pinki | Orange |

stimuli.title: Eight persons around a round table, with ages
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Akhilesh, Bhagwati, Deepti, Gurmeet, Jasoda, Kamlesh, Neetu and Sahil sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. Their ages are 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36, 39 and 42 years, one age each. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise.)

- Sahil sits opposite Akhilesh and is the oldest of all.
- Neetu is the youngest of all and sits immediately to the right of Akhilesh.
- Gurmeet sits second to the left of Sahil and is 18 years older than Neetu.
- Deepti sits immediately to the right of Sahil and is 3 years older than Neetu.
- Kamlesh sits opposite Gurmeet, and Jasoda sits immediately between Gurmeet and Sahil.
- Akhilesh is older than Bhagwati but younger than Kamlesh.
- Jasoda is 3 years younger than Bhagwati.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 7 anticlockwise from Akhilesh.
Step 1: Sahil = 4 (42). Neetu = 1 (21). Gurmeet, second to Sahil's left (clockwise): 2, aged 21 + 18 = 39. Deepti, to Sahil's right: 5, aged 24.
Step 2: Kamlesh is opposite Gurmeet: 6. Jasoda sits between Gurmeet (2) and Sahil (4): 3. Bhagwati = 7.
Step 3: 27, 30, 33 and 36 remain for Akhilesh, Bhagwati, Jasoda and Kamlesh. Jasoda = Bhagwati − 3 and Bhagwati < Akhilesh < Kamlesh: Jasoda 27, Bhagwati 30, Akhilesh 33, Kamlesh 36 (Jasoda 30, Bhagwati 33 would leave Akhilesh younger than Bhagwati).

| Seat | Person | Age |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Akhilesh | 33 |
| 1 | Neetu | 21 |
| 2 | Gurmeet | 39 |
| 3 | Jasoda | 27 |
| 4 | Sahil | 42 |
| 5 | Deepti | 24 |
| 6 | Kamlesh | 36 |
| 7 | Bhagwati | 30 |

stimuli.title: Eight persons seated in order of rank
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Aanya, Balwant, Darshana, Gitesh, Himmat, Kesar, Prachi and Shivam sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. They were ranked 1 to 8 in a test (rank 1 is the highest), and they are seated so that the person with each next rank (2 after 1, 3 after 2, and so on up to 8) sits third to the right of the person with the previous rank. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise.)

- Prachi sits second to the left of Himmat, and Shivam sits immediately to the right of Prachi.
- Gitesh sits opposite Kesar, and Aanya sits immediately to the left of Kesar.
- Balwant is ranked last, and Kesar is ranked below Darshana.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 7 anticlockwise from the rank-1 person. Moving three seats right each time, the ranks 1 to 8 sit at seats 0, 3, 6, 1, 4, 7, 2, 5. So seat 0 = rank 1, 1 = rank 4, 2 = rank 7, 3 = rank 2, 4 = rank 5, 5 = rank 8, 6 = rank 3, 7 = rank 6.
Step 1: Balwant (rank 8) = seat 5. Prachi, Shivam and Himmat sit in three consecutive seats p, p + 1, p + 2; Kesar, Aanya and Gitesh satisfy Aanya = Kesar − 1 and Gitesh = Kesar + 4.
Step 2: Avoiding seat 5, the only fits are (a) Prachi 0, Shivam 1, Himmat 2, Gitesh 3, Aanya 6, Kesar 7, Darshana 4, or (b) Prachi 1, Shivam 2, Himmat 3, Kesar 0, Aanya 7, Gitesh 4, Darshana 6.
Step 3: In (b) Kesar would be ranked 1, above Darshana (rank 3) ✗. So (a): Prachi 1, Gitesh 2, Aanya 3, Shivam 4, Darshana 5, Kesar 6, Himmat 7, Balwant 8.

| Seat | Person | Rank |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Prachi | 1 |
| 1 | Shivam | 4 |
| 2 | Himmat | 7 |
| 3 | Gitesh | 2 |
| 4 | Darshana | 5 |
| 5 | Balwant | 8 |
| 6 | Aanya | 3 |
| 7 | Kesar | 6 |

stimuli.title: Seven floors and seven fruits
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Bunty, Chikki, Golu, Jugnu, Minku, Pappu and Tinku live on the seven floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 7 the topmost). Each likes a different fruit among Apple, Banana, Grapes, Guava, Mango, Orange and Papaya.

- Minku lives on floor 4 and likes Orange.
- Chikki lives immediately above Minku, and Bunty lives immediately below Minku.
- Pappu lives on the topmost floor, and Jugnu lives between Chikki and Pappu.
- Golu lives below Tinku.
- The person who likes Mango lives immediately below the person who likes Orange, and the person who likes Grapes lives two floors above the Mango lover.
- The person on the topmost floor likes Papaya, and Golu likes Guava.
- Tinku does not like Banana.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Minku = 4 (Orange), Chikki = 5, Bunty = 3, Pappu = 7, Jugnu = 6 (between 5 and 7).
Step 2: Floors 1 and 2 remain for Golu and Tinku; Golu is below: Golu = 1, Tinku = 2.
Step 3: Mango is immediately below Orange: floor 3 (Bunty). Grapes is two floors above Mango: floor 5 (Chikki). Papaya: floor 7 (Pappu). Golu: Guava.
Step 4: Apple and Banana remain for Tinku (2) and Jugnu (6); Tinku does not like Banana: Tinku Apple, Jugnu Banana.

| Floor | Person | Fruit |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | Pappu | Papaya |
| 6 | Jugnu | Banana |
| 5 | Chikki | Grapes |
| 4 | Minku | Orange |
| 3 | Bunty | Mango |
| 2 | Tinku | Apple |
| 1 | Golu | Guava |

stimuli.title: Ten residents in a five-storey building with two flats per floor
stimuli.content:
Ten persons Ajit, Bimla, Chaman, Dharmesh, Ekam, Firoza, Gaurangi, Hardik, Ishita and Jaggi live in a five-storey building (floor 1 is the lowermost). Each floor has two flats, West and East; each West flat is directly above the West flat of the floor below, and likewise for the East flats. One person lives in each flat.

- Ajit lives in the West flat of floor 3, and Gaurangi lives in the other flat on his floor.
- Jaggi lives directly above Gaurangi, and Bimla lives directly above Jaggi.
- Hardik lives on the topmost floor, and Ekam lives directly below Hardik.
- Chaman lives in an East flat on a floor below Ajit's.
- Ishita lives on the lowermost floor, and Firoza lives directly above Dharmesh.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Ajit = 3 West, Gaurangi = 3 East, Jaggi = 4 East, Bimla = 5 East.
Step 2: Hardik is on floor 5; the East flat is Bimla's, so Hardik = 5 West and Ekam = 4 West.
Step 3: Chaman is in an East flat below floor 3: 1 East or 2 East. Firoza is directly above Dharmesh: the free stacked pairs are 1–2 West and 1–2 East, and the East pair would leave no East flat for Chaman, so Dharmesh = 1 West, Firoza = 2 West.
Step 4: Ishita is on floor 1: 1 East. Chaman = 2 East.

| Floor | West | East |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Hardik | Bimla |
| 4 | Ekam | Jaggi |
| 3 | Ajit | Gaurangi |
| 2 | Firoza | Chaman |
| 1 | Dharmesh | Ishita |

stimuli.title: Six floors, six pets and six drinks
stimuli.content:
Six persons Lakhan, Mili, Nirja, Omi, Rasika and Taran live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost). Each owns a different pet among a Cat, a Dog, a Fish, a Hamster, a Parrot and a Rabbit, and each drinks a different one of Coffee, Juice, Lassi, Milk, Soup and Tea.

- Lakhan lives on an even-numbered floor and owns the Cat.
- The Fish owner lives immediately below the Cat owner.
- Nirja lives on the topmost floor and drinks Lassi.
- Omi lives somewhere between Lakhan and Nirja.
- The Rabbit owner drinks Juice and lives immediately below the Lassi drinker.
- Taran lives on the lowermost floor and drinks Tea; Mili lives immediately above Taran and owns the Dog.
- Rasika drinks Coffee.
- The Hamster owner lives above the Parrot owner, and the Milk drinker lives above the Soup drinker.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Nirja = 6 (Lassi). Taran = 1 (Tea), Mili = 2 (Dog).
Step 2: The Rabbit owner, who drinks Juice, is on floor 5. Lakhan (Cat) is on an even floor: 4 (2 is Mili's), so the Fish is on floor 3.
Step 3: Omi lives between Lakhan (4) and Nirja (6): 5, so Omi owns the Rabbit and drinks Juice. Rasika = 3 (Fish) and drinks Coffee.
Step 4: Hamster and Parrot remain for Nirja (6) and Taran (1); the Hamster is higher: Nirja Hamster, Taran Parrot. Milk and Soup remain for Lakhan (4) and Mili (2); Milk is higher: Lakhan Milk, Mili Soup.

| Floor | Person | Pet | Drink |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | Nirja | Hamster | Lassi |
| 5 | Omi | Rabbit | Juice |
| 4 | Lakhan | Cat | Milk |
| 3 | Rasika | Fish | Coffee |
| 2 | Mili | Dog | Soup |
| 1 | Taran | Parrot | Tea |

stimuli.title: Five Greek capital letters for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, the Greek capital letters Γ, Λ, Ξ, Π and Ψ are used with these meanings:
'A Γ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A Λ B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A Ξ B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A Π B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'; 'A Ψ B' means 'A is equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: Γ means >, Λ means <, Ξ means ≥, Π means ≤ and Ψ means =. Rewrite the statements with ordinary signs, join them into a chain and test each conclusion.

stimuli.title: Five chess symbols defined by negations
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, chess symbols are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A ♔ B' means 'A is neither smaller than nor equal to B'; 'A ♕ B' means 'A is not greater than B'; 'A ♖ B' means 'A is neither greater than nor smaller than B'; 'A ♗ B' means 'A is not smaller than B'; 'A ♘ B' means 'A is neither greater than nor equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Translate each negation: 'neither smaller nor equal' = >, 'not greater' = ≤, 'neither greater nor smaller' = =, 'not smaller' = ≥, 'neither greater nor equal' = <. So ♔ is >, ♕ is ≤, ♖ is =, ♗ is ≥ and ♘ is <. Then join the statements into one chain.

stimuli.title: Six treks in six months, read by season
stimuli.content:
Six friends Aadi, Bela, Daksh, Hema, Ishan and Kajal each go on one trek in the same year, in six different months among January, March, April, July, October and December. Take the seasons as: Spring = January to March, Summer = April to June, Monsoon = July to September, Winter = October to December.

- Hema treks in the only Summer month among the six.
- Ishan treks in a Monsoon month.
- Kajal treks in the month that comes just before Hema's among the six months.
- Daksh and Bela both trek in Winter, and Bela's month is later.
stimuli.solution:
Of the six months, only April is in Summer: Hema. Only July is in Monsoon: Ishan. The month before April in the list is March: Kajal. Winter months are October and December; Bela is later, so Daksh October and Bela December. Aadi takes the remaining month, January.

Jan Aadi, Mar Kajal, Apr Hema, Jul Ishan, Oct Daksh, Dec Bela.

stimuli.title: Six appointments across the end of September 2026
stimuli.content:
Six persons Pranav, Rukmini, Sachin, Tanvi, Uttam and Vidya each have one appointment at a passport office on six different dates from Friday, 25 September 2026 to Tuesday, 6 October 2026 (September has 30 days).

- Rukmini's appointment is on the last day of September.
- Pranav's appointment is exactly five days after Rukmini's.
- Tanvi's appointment is on the first Saturday of the period.
- Vidya's appointment is on a Friday in October.
- Sachin's appointment is on the day after Vidya's.
- Uttam's appointment is on a Monday, before Rukmini's.
stimuli.solution:
Days: Fri 25, Sat 26, Sun 27, Mon 28, Tue 29, Wed 30 September; Thu 1, Fri 2, Sat 3, Sun 4, Mon 5, Tue 6 October. Rukmini 30 September; Pranav five days later, 5 October. Tanvi: first Saturday, 26 September. Vidya: the Friday in October, 2 October; Sachin 3 October. Uttam: a Monday before 30 September, 28 September.

Tanvi 26 Sep (Sat), Uttam 28 Sep (Mon), Rukmini 30 Sep (Wed), Vidya 2 Oct (Fri), Sachin 3 Oct (Sat), Pranav 5 Oct (Mon).

stimuli.title: Six employees and their retirement years
stimuli.content:
Six employees Gyan, Hridya, Kesar, Lohit, Mrinal and Navya of a bank were born in six different years between 1960 and 1995. Each employee retires in the year in which he or she turns 60.

- Kesar retires in 2031.
- Lohit is seven years younger than Kesar.
- Gyan retires in 2026, and Navya is exactly ten years younger than Gyan.
- Hridya was born in a leap year, after Kesar but before Lohit.
- Mrinal is the youngest of the six, and Mrinal's age in 2026 is a perfect square.
stimuli.solution:
Kesar: 2031 − 60 = 1971; Lohit 1978. Gyan: 2026 − 60 = 1966; Navya 1976. Hridya: a leap year after 1971 and before 1978 — 1972 or 1976 — and 1976 is Navya's, so 1972. Mrinal is the youngest (after 1978) and is a perfect-square age in 2026: 36 (born 1990) is the only one within 1979–1995 (25 would be 2001, 49 would be 1977).

Birth / retirement: Gyan 1966/2026, Kesar 1971/2031, Hridya 1972/2032, Navya 1976/2036, Lohit 1978/2038, Mrinal 1990/2050.

stimuli.title: Three departments, two posts each, six joining years
stimuli.content:
Six employees Aarav, Bhakti, Chaitali, Devesh, Eeshan and Fiza work in three departments of a company — HR, IT and Sales. Each holds one of two posts, Manager or Executive, and each joined in a different year from 2018 to 2023.

- Each department has exactly two of them: one Manager and one Executive, and in each department the Manager joined earlier than the Executive.
- Aarav, an Executive, joined last of the six.
- Devesh joined first of the six, and Bhakti works in the same department as Devesh.
- Fiza is a Manager and joined one year after Devesh.
- Chaitali works in Sales and joined in 2020.
- Eeshan joined in the year after Chaitali and works in the same department as her.
- Bhakti does not work in IT.
stimuli.solution:
Aarav joined in 2023 as an Executive; Devesh in 2018. Devesh joined before everyone, so he cannot be an Executive (his Manager would have joined earlier): Devesh is a Manager, and Bhakti, in his department, is its Executive. Fiza: Manager, 2019. Chaitali: Sales, 2020; Eeshan: Sales, 2021 — so Chaitali is the Sales Manager and Eeshan the Sales Executive. Sales is full, so Devesh and Bhakti are in HR or IT; Bhakti is not in IT, so both are in HR. Fiza then manages IT and Aarav is the IT Executive. Bhakti takes the remaining year, 2022.

HR: Devesh (Manager, 2018), Bhakti (Executive, 2022); IT: Fiza (Manager, 2019), Aarav (Executive, 2023); Sales: Chaitali (Manager, 2020), Eeshan (Executive, 2021).

stimuli.title: Five geometric codes for relations
stimuli.solution: Decode pair by pair from the left. Two children of the same person are siblings; a child's two parents are a married couple.

stimuli.title: A family of six across three generations
stimuli.content:
A family has six members — Gunjan, Harsh, Indira, Jatin, Kirti and Lavanya — across three generations, with exactly two married couples.

- Harsh is married to Indira.
- Gunjan is the only grandchild of Indira and is a girl.
- Lavanya is the daughter-in-law of Harsh.
- Jatin is the father of Gunjan.
- Kirti is unmarried and is the sister-in-law of Lavanya.
stimuli.solution:
Lavanya, Harsh's daughter-in-law, is married to a son of Harsh; Jatin is Gunjan's father and Gunjan is Indira's grandchild, so Jatin is that son and Lavanya his wife. Kirti is unmarried, so as Lavanya's sister-in-law she must be her husband's sister: Harsh's daughter.
Tree: Harsh + Indira → Jatin (+ Lavanya) → Gunjan; Kirti.

stimuli.title: A family of eight with two cousins
stimuli.content:
A family has eight members — Bhola, Charu, Divya, Eshan, Faiz, Gita, Hiten and Ira — across three generations, with three married couples. Every spouse is a member of the family.

- Bhola is Charu's husband, and Eshan is their only son.
- Divya is a daughter of Bhola.
- Faiz is the son-in-law of Bhola.
- Gita is the mother of Ira and the sister-in-law of Divya.
- Hiten (a boy) and Ira (a girl) are the only grandchildren of Charu, and they are cousins.
stimuli.solution:
Faiz, Bhola's son-in-law, is married to Bhola's daughter Divya (the only daughter in the family). Gita is Divya's sister-in-law and not Faiz's wife, so she is Eshan's wife; Ira's mother is Gita, so Ira is Eshan's daughter. Hiten, the other grandchild and Ira's cousin, is the son of Divya and Faiz.
Tree: Bhola + Charu → Divya (+ Faiz) → Hiten; Eshan (+ Gita) → Ira.

stimuli.title: Four coded two-word phrases
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'green tea' is written as 'mi lo'
'tea time' is written as 'ru mi'
'time flies' is written as 'ka ru'
'green leaf' is written as 'lo se'
(The codes of the words in a phrase may be in any order.)
stimuli.solution: tea = mi (phrases 1 and 2), time = ru (2 and 3), green = lo (1 and 4). Then flies = ka and leaf = se.

stimuli.solution: Count the letters, sort the consonants, count the vowels; letters of the word that are vowels do not appear in part (2).

stimuli.title: Six trees and their heights
stimuli.content:
Six trees P, Q, R, S, T and U in a garden have different heights.

- Tree R is taller than exactly four of the other trees.
- Tree Q is taller than tree T but shorter than tree U.
- Tree P is shorter than tree T.
- Exactly one tree is taller than tree S and shorter than tree R.
stimuli.solution: R is the 2nd tallest. U > Q > T > P, so U is the tallest. S is two places below R, that is, 4th tallest; Q, T and P fill the 3rd, 5th and 6th places in that order. Tallest to shortest: U, R, Q, S, T, P.

stimuli.title: A bite in the dark
stimuli.content:
Every year, thousands of people in rural India die after being bitten by snakes, and many more are left with damaged limbs. Most of the victims are farmers and farm workers, bitten while cutting crops, walking along field bunds at night or sleeping on the floor of their huts. The monsoon months, when rain floods the burrows of rats and drives out the snakes that hunt them, are the most dangerous.

Doctors say that most of these deaths can be prevented. An effective medicine, antivenom, has been available for decades and is produced in India. It works best when it is given early, ideally within a few hours of the bite. The tragedy is that many victims never reach a hospital in time.

One reason is distance. A village may be an hour or more from the nearest health centre that stocks antivenom. Another is belief. Many families first take the victim to a local healer, who may cut the wound, apply herbs or tie a tight cloth above the bite. Precious hours are lost, and some of these treatments cause harm of their own.

Health workers are trying to change this through simple advice. A person who has been bitten should stay calm and keep the bitten limb still, because movement helps the venom spread through the body. Rings and bangles should be removed before the limb swells. The victim should be carried, not made to walk, to a hospital as quickly as possible. Trying to suck out the venom or cutting the wound does no good.

Prevention matters too. Wearing boots in the fields, carrying a torch at night and sleeping on a raised cot rather than on the floor greatly reduce the risk. These are small habits, but in a country where snakes and people share the same fields, they can be the difference between life and death.

stimuli.title: Homes without an address
stimuli.content:
Ask for directions in many Indian towns and you will hear something like this: 'Go past the temple, turn left at the big neem tree, and ask for the house with the blue gate behind the flour mill.' For the people who live there, such directions work well enough. For anyone else, they can be a puzzle.

Millions of homes have no precise address. Streets may have no names, house numbers may be missing or follow no order, and the same name may be shared by two or three lanes. Local residents rarely notice the problem, because they know their neighbourhood by heart. It becomes serious only when a stranger must find a particular door quickly.

An ambulance driver is the most obvious example. Every minute he spends asking shopkeepers for directions is a minute lost for the patient. Fire engines and police vans face the same difficulty. Delivery companies also lose money: a parcel that cannot be delivered must be carried back, stored and sent out again, and some of that cost is passed on to customers.

The lack of an address can also shut people out. Opening a bank account, getting a gas connection or applying for a loan usually requires proof of where one lives. A family in an unnamed lane may find it hard to supply such proof, even if it has lived there for twenty years.

Several solutions are being tried. Some towns are naming streets and fixing number plates on every building. Others are testing digital codes that identify a small square of land from map coordinates, so that any location can be described by a short string of letters and numbers, even where there are no street names at all. Such codes do not depend on local knowledge, but they work only if people know their own code and the services that need it can read it.

An address, in short, is more than a line on an envelope. It is a way of being found.

stimuli.title: The first number in the room
stimuli.content:
In a well-known kind of experiment, people are asked to write down the last two digits of their phone number and then to say how much they would pay for an ordinary item, such as a box of chocolates or a cordless mouse. The digits have nothing to do with the item, and everyone knows it. Yet, again and again, those whose digits are high offer noticeably more than those whose digits are low. A number that should carry no weight has quietly pulled their judgement towards itself.

Psychologists call this anchoring. When we must estimate a value we are unsure of, we tend to start from whatever figure is in front of us and adjust from there, usually not far enough. The first number becomes an anchor, and our final answer stays within reach of its chain.

Sellers have long understood this. A shop that marks a sari at ₹6,000 and then 'reduces' it to ₹4,500 is not only offering a discount; it is fixing ₹6,000 in the buyer's mind as the true value, so that ₹4,500 feels like a gain, whatever the sari is really worth. In negotiations, too, the side that names the first figure often gains an advantage, because the discussion that follows tends to circle around it. A seller who opens high, within reason, usually settles higher than one who opens modestly.

Experts are not immune. In studies, experienced professionals asked to value a house or to fix a penalty have been swayed by figures they had been told were arbitrary. Knowing about the bias does not remove it, though it can weaken it.

The most practical defence is to set one's own anchor before hearing anyone else's. A buyer who has checked prices in three shops, or a borrower who has worked out what monthly instalment she can afford before visiting a lender, enters the conversation with a figure of her own. The other side's anchor still pulls, but now it pulls against something.

stimuli.title: The signature that binds
stimuli.content:
Few documents are signed as casually, or regretted as deeply, as a loan guarantee. A friend or relative needs a loan, the bank asks for a guarantor, and someone close to the borrower signs, often at the branch counter and often without reading the agreement. To the guarantor it feels like an act of friendship, a formality that costs nothing. It is, in fact, a promise to repay someone else's debt.

The promise is not a weak one. In India, as in many other countries, the law treats a guarantor's liability as co-extensive with that of the borrower. If the borrower defaults, the lender is generally free to demand the money from the guarantor without first suing the borrower or selling his property. Suppose a man borrows ₹5,00,000, repays ₹2,00,000 of the principal and then stops paying, leaving ₹30,000 of interest unpaid. The bank may ask his guarantor for ₹3,30,000, together with any further interest and charges it is entitled to recover.

The consequences reach beyond money. A default by the borrower can be reported against the guarantor as well, and a person who has guaranteed one large loan may find banks reluctant to lend to her, because part of her capacity to borrow is already spoken for. In this sense a guarantee is a latent debt: it does not appear in one's own accounts, but it can surface at any time.

Why, then, do so many people sign? Partly because refusing feels like an insult to the borrower. Partly because the risk seems remote: the borrower is a cousin with a steady job, or a friend whose business is doing well. Guarantees, however, are asked for precisely because lenders are not sure that the loan will be repaid.

None of this means that one should never stand guarantee. It means that a guarantee deserves the same scrutiny as a loan of one's own. A careful guarantor reads the agreement, asks how the borrower plans to repay, keeps track of whether instalments are being paid, and signs only for an amount she could afford to lose.

stimuli.title: Each generation's normal
stimuli.content:
Ask an elderly fisherman on almost any Indian coast about the sea of his youth, and he will describe catches that sound like exaggerations: nets so heavy that three men struggled to haul them in, fish as long as a man's arm, sharks seen close to the shore. Ask his grandson, who fishes the same waters today, and he will describe a good day that his grandfather would have called a poor one. Yet the grandson does not feel that anything has been lost. The sea he knows is the only sea he has known.

The fisheries scientist Daniel Pauly gave this pattern a name in the 1990s: the shifting baseline. Each generation, he argued, takes the state of the world it first encounters as normal, and measures decline only from that point. Losses that happened before its time are invisible to it. Over several generations, a resource can be reduced to a fraction of its former abundance without any single generation witnessing a dramatic collapse.

The idea reaches well beyond fishing. City dwellers who grew up under a hazy sky may regard a few clear days as unusually good rather than as what the sky once was. Birdwatchers who began counting a species when it was already scarce may record no fall at all. Even official targets can be affected: a plan to 'restore' a river to its condition of thirty years ago may aim at a state that was itself badly degraded.

The difficulty is partly one of evidence. Older conditions were seldom measured with the care that today's surveys demand, and memories, as critics rightly point out, can be selective or romantic. An old man's recollection of giant fish is not data. But dismissing such accounts altogether carries its own risk, since it leaves the most recent, and most depleted, state as the only one that counts.

Researchers have therefore turned to unconventional sources: old photographs of fishermen posing with their catch, market records, colonial gazetteers, even the menus of restaurants. None of these is precise, but together they can show the direction and rough size of a change that no living observer can see in full.

The lesson is not that the past was always better. It is that our sense of what is normal is borrowed from a short span of experience, and that a society which wishes to protect what remains must first find out what has already gone.

stimuli.title: A string with an edge
stimuli.content:
On festival days in many towns, the sky fills with kites, and on the rooftops below, children and adults battle to cut one another's strings. To win these contests, many fliers use a string coated with powdered glass. Such a string can (1) ______ through a rival's thread in seconds, and the winner's shout of triumph rings across the lanes.

The same sharpness makes it dangerous. Every season, thousands of birds, especially pigeons and black kites, fly into loose strings that hang from trees, poles and wires, and many of them die of their (2) ______. Strings stretched across roads have also cut the necks of people riding two-wheelers, sometimes fatally.

Several states have banned glass-coated string, and some cities have gone further, banning strings made of nylon and other synthetic materials, which do not snap easily. Yet the ban is hard to (3) ______. The string is cheap, it is sold quietly from small shops and homes, and demand rises sharply in the few days before the festival, when the police have many other duties.

Volunteers have stepped in where the law falls short. In some cities, groups set up bird-rescue camps where vets stitch the wounds of injured birds and release them once they have healed. Others go from roof to roof after the festival, collecting the tangled string that would otherwise (4) ______ hanging from trees and wires for months.

Many riders now fix a thin metal rod in front of the handlebar of their scooters, which catches any string before it reaches the rider's neck. Such rods help, but doctors and police (5) ______ that the safest solution is a simple one: fly kites with plain cotton thread, which breaks long before it can wound.

stimuli.title: The case for the roundabout
stimuli.content:
At a busy crossroads controlled by traffic lights, drivers spend much of their time waiting. Even when no vehicle is coming from any other direction, a red light holds them back until it (1) ______. A well-designed roundabout works differently. Vehicles entering it give way to the traffic already circling and then move on as soon as there is a gap, so that at quiet hours almost nobody has to stop at all.

Safety experts value roundabouts for a further reason. At an ordinary crossing, the most serious crashes are side-on or head-on collisions between vehicles moving at speed. A roundabout (2) ______ such crashes almost impossible: all traffic moves in one direction, and the curve forces drivers to slow down. Accidents still happen, but they tend to be minor scrapes rather than deadly impacts.

Roundabouts are not a cure for every junction, however. When traffic is very heavy on one road and light on the others, the busy stream may never leave a gap, and vehicles on the quieter roads can wait for a long time. Large roundabouts can also be hard for pedestrians and cyclists to (3) ______, since there is no pause in the flow of vehicles. In many cities, such circles have been fitted with traffic lights for the rush hours, which (4) ______ much of their advantage.

Much also depends on drivers. A roundabout works only if those entering it actually give way. Where drivers push in regardless, the circle quickly becomes a knot of vehicles, each blocking the next. Engineers therefore stress that good design must be (5) ______ by clear signs, road markings and the steady enforcement of one simple rule: give way to the traffic already on the circle.

stimuli.title: Holes that come back
stimuli.content:
Every monsoon, the roads of many Indian cities break out in potholes. They appear so **(1) regularly** that many residents treat them as a season of their own, like the rains that bring them. Yet potholes are not an act of nature. Engineers say that most of them can be traced to two causes: water and poor construction.

A road surface is meant to shed rain into the drains along its edges. When the surface is laid without the proper slope, or when the drains are **(2) cleared**, water stands on the road and slowly seeps into small cracks. Heavy vehicles passing over the weakened patch press the water down and force it out again, loosening the stones beneath. Within days a crack can **(3) shrink** into a hole deep enough to throw a rider off a scooter.

The usual response makes matters worse. Crews arrive after the rains, shovel loose material into the hole and press it down with a roller or even with their feet. Such patches are cheap and quick, but they rarely bond with the old surface, and the next heavy shower washes them out. The city then pays for the same hole again and again, a cycle that some critics believe is **(4) convenient** for contractors.

Better methods exist. A pothole can be cut into a neat rectangle, cleaned, dried and filled with material that is pressed down in thin layers, so that the repair **(5) crumbles** for years. Some cities also write a defect liability period into road contracts, under which the contractor must repair, at his own cost, any damage that appears within a fixed number of years. Where such clauses are **(6) ignored**, contractors have a reason to build well the first time.

Residents can help too. Several cities now allow people to photograph a pothole and report it through an app, and some publish how quickly each complaint is closed. Records of this kind make it harder for the same hole to be patched, forgotten and paid for, year after year.

stimuli.title: Error checks on a cash-recycler link
stimuli.content:
A branch's cash-recycling machine talks to its controller over a serial link that uses two error checks.

**Check 1 - code words.** Each command is sent as one of only four valid 6-bit code words:

| Command | Code word |
|---|---|
| IDLE | 000000 |
| COUNT | 001111 |
| DISPENSE | 110011 |
| LOCK | 111100 |

The Hamming distance between two words is the number of bit positions in which they differ. A received word that is not valid is corrected to the nearest valid code word.

**Check 2 - CRC.** Status messages are 4 bits long. The sender appends 3 zeros to the message, divides the result by the generator 1011 using modulo-2 (XOR) division with no carries or borrows, and appends the 3-bit remainder to the message as the CRC.
stimuli.solution: Every pair of valid code words differs in exactly 4 positions, so the minimum distance is 4: up to 3 bit errors are always detected and 1 bit error can always be corrected. 011111 is 1 bit from COUNT (001111). For the message 1101, 1101000 divided by 1011 leaves the remainder 001, so 1101001 is sent.

stimuli.title: CCTV recording system of a branch
stimuli.content:
A branch installs a CCTV system. All figures use decimal units (1 GB = 1,000 MB, 1 TB = 1,000 GB, 1 byte = 8 bits).

| Item | Specification |
|---|---|
| Cameras | 8 IP cameras, each streaming continuously at a constant 4 Mbps (megabits per second) |
| Recorder | Network video recorder (NVR) that records all streams 24 hours a day |
| NVR storage | 6 hard disks of 4 TB each, configured as RAID 6 (two disks' worth of capacity used for parity) |
| Head-office link | 50 Mbps link used to view the cameras live from the regional office |
| Policy | When the disks are full, the oldest recording is overwritten |
stimuli.solution: Total stream = 8 x 4 = 32 Mbps. Per day: 32 Mbps x 86,400 s = 2,764,800 Mb = 345,600 MB = 345.6 GB. RAID 6 usable capacity = (6 - 2) x 4 = 16 TB, and the array survives any two simultaneous disk failures. Retention = 16,000 / 345.6 = 46.3, so 46 full days are kept.

stimuli.title: Firewall rules of a branch
stimuli.content:
A branch firewall checks each new connection against these rules from top to bottom and applies the FIRST rule that matches (protocol, source, destination and destination port must all match). A connection that matches no rule is dropped. The firewall is stateful.

| Rule | Action | Protocol | Source | Destination | Destination port |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Allow | TCP | 10.20.30.0/24 | any | 443 |
| 2 | Deny | TCP | any | any | 3389 |
| 3 | Allow | TCP | 10.20.30.10 | 10.20.0.0/16 | 3389 |
| 4 | Allow | TCP | 10.20.30.0/24 | 10.20.0.25 | 993 |
| 5 | Allow | UDP | 10.20.30.0/24 | 10.20.0.53 | 53 |

The branch LAN is 10.20.30.0/24; head-office servers are in 10.20.0.0/16.
stimuli.solution: Rules are matched in order, so rule 2 blocks all RDP (port 3389) before rule 3 is ever reached; rule 3 must be moved above rule 2. Traffic matching no rule meets the implicit deny. A stateful firewall remembers allowed connections and lets their reply packets back in automatically. Port 993 is IMAP over TLS.

stimuli.title: Complaints received at a bank's cyber cell
stimuli.content:
The cyber cell of a bank logged these four complaints in one week:

1. **Customer Mr. P** got a call from someone claiming to be from the bank's 'KYC team', who asked him to install a 'support app' from the app store and read out a code shown in it. Moments later, the caller could see Mr. P's phone screen, watched him open his banking app, and money was transferred out.
2. **The bank's accounts team** received an email that looked like it came from a regular stationery supplier, from the domain supp1ier-mart.example instead of supplier-mart.example. It said the supplier's bank account had changed and asked that the pending invoice be paid to the new account. The team paid Rs 4.8 lakh.
3. **A branch manager** received a phone call in a voice that sounded exactly like the regional head's, urgently asking her to release a large payment before an audit. The regional head later confirmed he never called; the voice had been generated by software trained on his speeches posted online.
4. **Several customers** of an online store found their card details misused. The store's site was genuine and used HTTPS, but investigators found that attackers had inserted a small JavaScript file into the checkout page that copied card details as they were typed and sent them to the attackers' server.
stimuli.solution: 1: remote-access (screen-sharing) app fraud. 2: business email compromise using a look-alike domain. 3: deepfake voice cloning (AI-generated vishing). 4: formjacking / digital (web) skimming of a checkout page.

stimuli.title: Excel ATM cash-loading register
stimuli.content:
A branch keeps this register in Excel (dates are real Excel dates; amounts are in rupees):

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
1,296 ÷ 36 × ? − 17² = 23 × 9 + 8

solution.concept: Work ÷ and × from left to right before − ; then undo the steps to find ?
solution.why_others_wrong: With 13, 15 or 16 the left side becomes 179, 251 or 287, not 215.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?)?
(3.6 × 0.25 + 0.45) ÷ 0.027 = ?

solution.concept: Finish the bracket first; then remove the decimals by scaling numerator and denominator alike
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 and 500 misplace the decimal point when dividing by 0.027; 17.57 ignores the bracket and divides only 0.45 by 0.027 (0.9 + 16.67).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the smallest perfect square that is exactly divisible by each of 6, 10 and 14?

solution.concept: Find the LCM, then make every prime power in it even
solution.explanation: LCM(6, 10, 14) = 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 210. Each prime appears once, so multiply by 210 again: 210² = 44,100 is the smallest perfect square divisible by all three.
steps: Every prime power must be even
solution.why_others_wrong: 210 is the LCM but not a perfect square; 1,764 = 42² is not divisible by 10; 900 = 30² is not divisible by 14.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If 7^(x − 2) = 343, what is the value of (x + 1)²?

solution.concept: Write 343 as a power of 7 and compare the indices
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 is x² rather than (x + 1)²; 16 takes x = 3 (the index of 343, forgetting the − 2); 49 uses x + 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Simplify: (xᵃ ÷ xᵇ)^(a + b) × (xᵇ ÷ xᶜ)^(b + c) × (xᶜ ÷ xᵃ)^(c + a), where x > 0.

solution.concept: (xᵐ)ⁿ = x^(mn), and the indices of a product add
solution.explanation: The first factor is x^((a − b)(a + b)) = x^(a² − b²). Likewise the others are x^(b² − c²) and x^(c² − a²). The indices add to a² − b² + b² − c² + c² − a² = 0, so the product is x⁰ = 1.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 confuses x⁰ with 0; x^(a + b + c) and x^(2a + 2b + 2c) add the outer indices instead of multiplying (a − b) by (a + b).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the value of 1.272727… ÷ 0.363636…, where the digits 27 and 36 recur without end?

solution.concept: A two-digit recurring block ab equals ab/99
solution.why_others_wrong: 127/36 writes 1.2727… as 127/99; 13/4 uses 90 instead of 99 as the denominator; 7/4 halves the correct value, as if the divisor were 0.7272….

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If x = ∛2 + ∛4, what is the value of x³ − 6x?

solution.explanation: Let a = ∛2 and b = ∛4. Then a³ = 2, b³ = 4 and ab = ∛8 = 2. So x³ = 2 + 4 + 3 × 2 × x = 6 + 6x, and x³ − 6x = 6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 drops a³ + b³; 2 keeps only a³; 12 counts a³ + b³ twice.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Express √(2√(2√(2√2))) as a power of 2.

solution.concept: Work from the innermost root outwards: √(2 × 2ᵏ) = 2^((1 + k)/2)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2^(7/8) stops one root early; 2^(31/32) takes one root too many; 2 is the limit of the endless pattern, not this four-root value.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If √(x + 16) + √(x − 5) = 7, what is the value of x?

solution.concept: Let a = √(x + 16), b = √(x − 5): a² − b² = 21 and a + b = 7, so a − b = 3
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 gives √36 + √15 ≈ 9.87; 4 makes x − 5 negative; 11 gives √27 + √6 ≈ 7.65.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
11.98% of 2,500.3 + 3/8 of 639.7 ≈ ?

solution.concept: Round each number to the nearest convenient value, then work out the percentage and the fraction

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
√1,849.3 × ∛3,374.6 − 19.98² ≈ ?

solution.concept: Recognise the perfect square, cube and square near each number
solution.why_others_wrong: 202 takes ∛3,375 as 14 (43 × 14 − 400); 1,045 adds 20² instead of subtracting it; 645 forgets 20².

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(? × 12.03) ÷ 7.98 ≈ 39.02 × 2.01 + 11.97

solution.concept: Simplify the right side first, then undo the × 12 and ÷ 8
solution.why_others_wrong: 135 inverts the operations (90 × 12 ÷ 8); 90 is the right side itself; 7.5 divides 90 by 12 and forgets to multiply by 8.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?% of 1,249.8 ≈ 418.1 − 13.98 × 11.97

solution.concept: Find the right side first, then express it as a percentage of 1,250
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 divides 250 by 1,000 instead of 1,250; 33 ignores the product (418 ÷ 1,250); 47 adds 168 instead of subtracting it (586 ÷ 1,250).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
∛(? + 6.02) ≈ 2.998² − √25.01

solution.concept: Evaluate the right side, cube it, and then subtract 6
solution.explanation: Right side ≈ 9 − 5 = 4. So ? + 6 ≈ 4³ = 64, and ? ≈ 58.
solution.why_others_wrong: 64 forgets to subtract 6; 70 adds 6 instead; 10 squares 4 instead of cubing it (16 − 6).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
(? − 23.98% of 450.2) ÷ 7.02 ≈ 20.98² ÷ 6.99 + 13.02

solution.concept: Simplify the right side, multiply back by 7, then add back the percentage
solution.why_others_wrong: 532 forgets to add back 24% of 450; 424 subtracts 108 instead of adding it; 700 takes 24% of 450 as 168.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
√? × 3.99 + 15.98² ≈ 33.03 × 11.98 − √1,296.2

solution.concept: Collect the known terms on one side, find √? and then square it
solution.why_others_wrong: 576 and 784 are 24² and 28², from slips of 8 in the subtraction; 26 is √?, not ?.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?% of 4,799.6 − 18.03% of 1,999.7 ≈ 21.98% of 2,700.4

solution.concept: Move the known percentage to the right side, then divide by 48 (1% of 4,800)
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 takes 18% of 2,000 as 180 (774 ÷ 48); 24 divides 954 by 40 instead of 48; 12 leaves out the 18% term (594 ÷ 48).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What approximate value should come in place of the question mark (?)?
?² + 7.02 × ? ≈ 29.98 × 12.02 + 8.97 × 10.03   (? is positive)

solution.concept: Round the right side, then look for a positive number with ? × (? + 7) equal to it
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 gives 15 × 22 = 330; 21 gives 21 × 28 = 588; 25 is the other factor of 450, not the value of ?.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ?

solution.concept: The differences grow by 1 each time: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, …
solution.explanation: 1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 2 = 4, 4 + 3 = 7, 7 + 4 = 11, 11 + 5 = 16. The next difference is 6, so the term is 16 + 6 = 22.
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 adds 5 again; 32 doubles 16; 25 adds 9, the sum of the last two differences.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
2, 6, 22, 86, 342, ?

solution.concept: Each term is 4 times the previous term minus 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,368 multiplies by 4 but does not subtract 2; 1,370 adds 2 instead; 1,026 multiplies by 3.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
196, 169, 144, 121, 100, ?

solution.concept: The terms are the squares of 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, … in falling order
solution.why_others_wrong: 79 subtracts 21 again (the last difference); 64 = 8² skips 9²; 90 subtracts 10, the square root of 100.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
90, 83, 69, ?, 20, −15

solution.concept: The amounts subtracted are multiples of 7: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 subtracts 14 again; 41 subtracts 28 too early; 62 subtracts only 7. None of them gives 20 after the next step.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
5, 6, 14, 41, 105, ?

solution.why_others_wrong: 169 adds 64 again; 210 doubles 105; 186 adds 9² = 81, taking the differences as squares.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
10, 19, 34, 59, 102, ?

solution.concept: Each term is twice the previous term minus 1², 2², 3², 4², …
solution.why_others_wrong: 168 subtracts 6² = 36 and skips 5²; 204 doubles without subtracting; 145 adds 43, the last term minus the one before it.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 14, 39, 84, 155, ?

solution.concept: Each term is n³ + n² + n for n = 1, 2, 3, …
steps: n³ + n² + n for n = 1 to 5
solution.shortcut: Differences 11, 25, 45, 71 have second differences 14, 20, 26 (rising by 6); next 32, so the next difference is 103.
solution.why_others_wrong: 252 leaves out the + n; 222 leaves out n²; 246 keeps the second difference at 20 instead of raising it to 32.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
2, 8, 24, ?, 160, 384

solution.why_others_wrong: 48 doubles 24 and 72 triples it, but neither leads on to 160 by one rule; 56 adds 32, which breaks the pattern of the later terms.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
7, 9, 15, 33, 87, 249, ?

solution.concept: The differences are multiplied by 3 each time: 2, 6, 18, 54, 162, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 411 adds 162 again; 747 triples the term instead of the difference; 573 only doubles the last difference (+324).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 5, 22, 91, 368, ?

solution.concept: Each term is 4 times the previous term plus 1, 2, 3, 4, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,476 adds 4 again; 1,472 multiplies by 4 and adds nothing; 1,840 multiplies by 5.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
4, 7, 13, 24, 42, 69, ?

solution.concept: The differences are 2 more than the squares: 1 + 2, 4 + 2, 9 + 2, 16 + 2, …
solution.explanation: Differences: 3, 6, 11, 18, 27 = 1² + 2, 2² + 2, 3² + 2, 4² + 2, 5² + 2. The next is 6² + 2 = 38, so the term is 69 + 38 = 107.
solution.why_others_wrong: 96 adds 27 again; 105 adds 36 and forgets the + 2; 111 adds the previous term (42 + 69).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
2, 6, 30, ?, 2,310, 30,030

solution.concept: Each term is the previous term multiplied by the next prime: × 3, × 5, × 7, × 11, × 13
solution.why_others_wrong: 180, 240 and 270 multiply 30 by 6, 8 and 9, which are not the next prime, and none of them gives 2,310 when multiplied by 11.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
2, 5, 18, 65, 218, ?

solution.concept: Each term is 3ⁿ − n² for n = 1, 2, 3, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 723 subtracts 6 instead of 6²; 765 adds 36; 654 only triples 218, ignoring the squares.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
100, 99, 96, 90, 80, 65, ?

solution.concept: The amounts subtracted are the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, …
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 subtracts 15 again; 45 subtracts 20 (taking the steps to rise by 5); 37 subtracts 28 and skips 21.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
1, 2, 3, 7, 22, 155, ?

solution.concept: From the third term on, each term is the product of the two terms before it, plus 1
solution.why_others_wrong: 3,410 forgets the + 1; 3,412 adds 2; 3,565 multiplies 155 by 23 (one more than 22).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the missing number (?) in the series:
5, 13, 35, ?, 275, 793

solution.why_others_wrong: 81 is 3⁴ alone; 105 triples 35 without subtracting 8; 89 subtracts 16 one step too early. None of them leads to 275.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
64, 32, 96, 24, 120, 20, ?

solution.concept: Divide by 2, multiply by 3, divide by 4, multiply by 5, … (the operations alternate and the numbers rise)
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 multiplies by 6 instead of 7; 160 multiplies by 8; 100 multiplies by 5 again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following series?
3, 16, 45, 96, 175, ?

solution.concept: Each term is n² × (n + 2) for n = 1, 2, 3, …
solution.shortcut: Differences 13, 29, 51, 79 have second differences 16, 22, 28; next 34, so the next difference is 113.
solution.why_others_wrong: 252 multiplies 36 by 7 (n + 1); 324 multiplies by 9 (n + 3); 276 keeps the second difference at 22.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
3, 10, 24, 52, 106, 220, 444

solution.concept: Each term is twice the previous term plus 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 10, 52 and 444 all fit; 220 confirms 108, since 106 × 2 + 4 = 216.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 2, 5, 16, 66, 326, 1,957

solution.concept: Multiply by 1, 2, 3, 4, … and add 1 each time
solution.why_others_wrong: 5, 16 and 326 fit; 326 confirms 65, since 66 × 5 + 1 = 331.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
1, 4, 20, 96, 600, 4,320, 35,280

solution.concept: Each term is n × n! (equivalently (n + 1)! − n!)
solution.why_others_wrong: 4, 96 and 4,320 are 2 × 2!, 4 × 4! and 6 × 6!; only 20 breaks the rule.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the wrong number in the series:
2, 3, 7, 25, 121, 723, 5,041

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve equations I and II and choose the relation between x and y that holds for every pair of roots.
I. x² − 25x + 156 = 0
II. y² − 20y + 96 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise; a root shared by both equations makes the relation non-strict
solution.explanation: I: (x − 12)(x − 13) = 0, so x = 12 or 13. II: (y − 8)(y − 12) = 0, so y = 8 or 12. The smallest x (12) equals the largest y (12), and every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for the pair x = y = 12; x < y holds for no pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Each quadratic below has two negative roots. Factorise both and decide which relation holds.
I. x² + 15x + 56 = 0
II. y² + 10y + 24 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise both; with negative roots, the larger number is the one nearer zero
solution.explanation: I: (x + 7)(x + 8) = 0, so x = −7 or −8. II: (y + 4)(y + 6) = 0, so y = −4 or −6. The largest x (−7) is below the smallest y (−6), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y treat 7 and 8 as larger than 4 and 6, ignoring the minus signs.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Find the roots of I and II and decide which relation between x and y, if any, always holds.
I. x² − x − 42 = 0
II. y² − 14y + 45 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: When one set of roots straddles the other, no single relation holds for every pair
solution.explanation: I: (x − 7)(x + 6) = 0, so x = 7 or −6. II: (y − 5)(y − 9) = 0, so y = 5 or 9. x = 7 is greater than y = 5 but less than y = 9, so no relation holds for every pair.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for 7 and 9; x < y fails for 7 and 5; x ≤ y and x ≥ y fail for the same pairs.
solution.final_answer: Option A: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 2x − 48 = 0
II. y² + 14y + 48 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise; compare the smallest x with the largest y
solution.explanation: I: (x − 8)(x + 6) = 0, so x = 8 or −6. II: (y + 6)(y + 8) = 0, so y = −6 or −8. The smallest x (−6) equals the largest y (−6), and every other pair has x > y. So x ≥ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y fails for the pair x = y = −6; x ≤ y holds only for that one pair.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I has a positive and a negative root, while II has two positive roots. Which relation between x and y holds?
I. x² + 7x − 60 = 0
II. y² − 26y + 168 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Factorise each equation; compare the largest x with the smallest y
solution.explanation: I: (x + 12)(x − 5) = 0, so x = 5 or −12. II: (y − 12)(y − 14) = 0, so y = 12 or 14. The largest x (5) is below the smallest y (12), so x < y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x > y and x ≥ y take x = 12 from I (the root is −12, not 12).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation II is a perfect square. Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 30x + 221 = 0
II. y² − 34y + 289 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: A perfect-square quadratic has one repeated root
solution.explanation: I: (x − 13)(x − 17) = 0, so x = 13 or 17. II: (y − 17)² = 0, so y = 17 only. x = 17 equals y and x = 13 is less than y. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for x = 17; x ≥ y fails for x = 13.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I is linear and equation II is quadratic. Solve both and choose the relation between x and y.
I. 3(x + 4) − 2(x − 1) = 2x − 6
II. y² − 41y + 420 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Expand and solve the linear equation; factorise the quadratic
solution.explanation: I: 3x + 12 − 2x + 2 = 2x − 6, so x + 14 = 2x − 6 and x = 20. II: (y − 20)(y − 21) = 0, so y = 20 or 21. x = 20 equals one value of y and is less than the other. So x ≤ y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y fails for y = 20; x > y holds for no value of y.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I looks quadratic. Simplify it, solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. (x + 2)(x + 3) = (x − 1)² + 25
II. y² + y − 2 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: The x² terms cancel, so equation I is really linear
solution.explanation: I: x² + 5x + 6 = x² − 2x + 1 + 25, so 7x = 20 and x = 20/7 ≈ 2.86. II: (y + 2)(y − 1) = 0, so y = 1 or −2. x ≈ 2.86 exceeds both values of y, so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y would need x to be at most 1; treating I as a quadratic invents a second root that does not exist.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text:
Equation I has an irrational coefficient (√3 ≈ 1.732). Solve both equations and choose the relation between x and y.
I. x² − 4√3x + 9 = 0
II. y² − 2y + 1 = 0

options.text: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

solution.concept: Use the quadratic formula (or split 4√3x = 3√3x + √3x); II is a perfect square
solution.explanation: I: discriminant = 48 − 36 = 12, so x = (4√3 ± 2√3)/2 = 3√3 or √3, that is about 5.20 or 1.73. II: (y − 1)² = 0, so y = 1. Both values of x exceed 1, so x > y.
solution.why_others_wrong: x < y and x ≤ y fail because even the smaller root √3 is above 1; no root is shared, so the relation is strict.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The five-digit number 35x72, where x is a digit, is divisible by 9. What is x?

solution.concept: A number is divisible by 9 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 9
solution.explanation: Digit sum = 3 + 5 + x + 7 + 2 = 17 + x. The only digit that makes this a multiple of 9 is x = 1 (sum 18).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 gives a digit sum of 17, 8 gives 25 and 4 gives 21; none is a multiple of 9 (21 is only a multiple of 3).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 2,341 × 4,567 × 1,234 is divided by 9?

solution.concept: A number leaves the same remainder on division by 9 as its digit sum; remainders of a product multiply
solution.explanation: 2,341 → 2 + 3 + 4 + 1 = 10 → remainder 1. 4,567 → 22 → remainder 4. 1,234 → 10 → remainder 1. So the product leaves 1 × 4 × 1 = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 is the remainder of the sum 2,341 + 4,567 + 1,234, not of the product; 0 and 1 would need a factor divisible by 9 or every remainder to be 1.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the LCM of the fractions 3/4, 5/6 and 9/10?

solution.concept: LCM of fractions = LCM of the numerators ÷ HCF of the denominators
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 is a common multiple but not the least (45/2 already works); 1/60 is HCF of numerators ÷ LCM of denominators, the formula for the HCF; 135/2 uses the product 3 × 5 × 9 instead of the LCM.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: How many divisors of 10,800 are multiples of 15?

solution.concept: A divisor that is a multiple of 15 is 15 × (a divisor of 10,800 ÷ 15)
solution.explanation: 10,800 = 2⁴ × 3³ × 5². A multiple of 15 must contain at least one 3 and one 5, so it is 15 × k with k a divisor of 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5. Number of such k = (4 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 30.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 is the number of all divisors of 10,800; 24 counts the divisors of 720 as (4)(3)(2); 45 uses the exponents of 10,800 with only the 5 reduced, (5)(3)(3).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 28! (the product 1 × 2 × 3 × … × 28) is divided by 29?

solution.concept: Wilson's theorem: for a prime p, (p − 1)! leaves remainder p − 1 when divided by p
solution.explanation: 29 is prime, so 28! = (29 − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod 29). A remainder of −1 is the same as 29 − 1 = 28.
solution.shortcut: Pair each number from 2 to 27 with its inverse mod 29: the pairs multiply to 1, leaving 1 × 28 ≡ 28.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 is the remainder of 27!, which forgets the factor 28; 0 would need 29 to divide 28!, but 29 is a prime larger than every factor; 27 subtracts 2 instead of 1 from 29.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A bank's loan book is ₹48 crore, and 3.5% of it is classified as non-performing. How much is non-performing, in lakh rupees? (1 crore = 100 lakh)

solution.concept: Find the percentage in crore, then convert: 1 crore = 100 lakh
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹16.8 lakh and ₹1,680 lakh use 10 and 1,000 lakh to a crore; ₹1.68 lakh is the answer in crore with the wrong unit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Neha's monthly salary is ₹50,000. 10% of it is deducted for her provident fund. She spends 70% of the remaining (take-home) amount and saves the rest. How much does she save a month?

solution.concept: Work on the take-home pay, not the gross salary
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹15,000 takes 30% of the gross salary; ₹10,000 subtracts the 10% deduction from 30% (20% of ₹50,000); ₹31,500 is what she spends.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A number is increased by 20% and the result is then increased by 25%. The final value is 120 more than the original number. What is the original number?

solution.explanation: After both increases the number is 1.2 × 1.25 = 1.5 times the original, that is 50% more. 50% of the number = 120, so the number is 240.
solution.why_others_wrong: 267 adds the rates to 45%; 200 takes the increase as 60%; 480 takes it as 25%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A village has 12,000 people, 60% of whom are adults. Over a year the number of adults rises by 5% and the number of children falls by 10%. What is the population at the end of the year?

solution.concept: Apply each rate to its own group and add
solution.why_others_wrong: 11,400 applies a net −5% to everyone; 11,520 swaps the groups (takes adults as 40%); 12,360 forgets the fall in the number of children.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: When the numerator of a fraction is increased by 20% and its denominator is decreased by 10%, the fraction becomes 16/15. What was the original fraction?

solution.explanation: New fraction = original × 1.2/0.9 = original × 4/3. So original = 16/15 × 3/4 = 4/5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8/9 undoes only the numerator change (÷ 1.2); 24/25 undoes only the denominator change (× 0.9); 32/25 multiplies by 1.2 instead of dividing.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The price of an item is increased by x% and the new price is then increased by 2x%. Overall the price rises by 32%. What is x?

solution.concept: Write the two changes as factors: (1 + x/100)(1 + 2x/100) = 1.32
solution.explanation: Try x = 10: 1.10 × 1.20 = 1.32 ✓. (Algebraically 2x² + 300x − 3,200 = 0 gives x = 10, the positive root.)

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A machine depreciates by 10% a year in each of the first two years and by 20% in the third year, each time on its value at the start of that year. Its total loss in value over the three years is ₹1,40,800. What was its original value?

solution.concept: Value after 3 years = original × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.8; the loss is the rest
solution.explanation: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.648, so the machine loses 35.2% of its value. 35.2% of the original = ₹1,40,800, giving original = 1,40,800 ÷ 0.352 = ₹4,00,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,52,000 adds the rates (40%); ₹3,20,000 takes the loss as 44%; ₹4,40,000 takes it as 32%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: ₹2,880 is divided between Asha and Bina in the ratio 7 : 9. How much more does Bina get than Asha?

solution.concept: Total parts = 7 + 9 = 16; the difference is 9 − 7 = 2 parts
solution.explanation: One part = 2,880 ÷ 16 = ₹180. Bina gets 2 parts more, that is ₹360.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,260 and ₹1,620 are Asha's and Bina's shares; ₹180 is one part, not the two-part difference.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A earns ₹36,000 a month and B earns ₹48,000. Each gets a raise of ₹6,000 a month. What is the new ratio of their salaries?

solution.concept: Add the raise to each salary first; a ratio does not stay the same when equal amounts are added
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 4 is the old ratio; 9 : 7 reverses the new one; 4 : 5 adds ₹12,000 to each salary.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The present ages of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 4. Eight years from now the ratio will be 7 : 9. What was the sum of their ages 4 years ago?

solution.concept: Let the ages be 3k and 4k and use the future ratio to find k
solution.explanation: 9(3k + 8) = 7(4k + 8) gives 27k + 72 = 28k + 56, so k = 16. Ages now: 48 and 64, sum 112. Four years ago the sum was 112 − 8 = 104.
solution.why_others_wrong: 112 is the present sum; 120 is the sum 4 years from now; 96 is the sum 8 years ago.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If (a + b) : (a − b) = 11 : 3, what is (a² + b²) : (a² − b²)?

solution.explanation: a : b = 14 : 8 = 7 : 4. Then a² + b² = 49 + 16 = 65 and a² − b² = 49 − 16 = 33 (in the same units), so the ratio is 65 : 33.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11 : 3 is the given ratio, not the one asked; 121 : 9 squares the given ratio; 33 : 65 is inverted.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A sum of money was to be divided among A, B and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4, but by mistake it was divided in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5. As a result C got ₹300 less than his due share. What was the sum?

solution.concept: C's due share is 4/9 of the sum and he got 5/12 of it
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,600, ₹5,400 and ₹7,200 multiply ₹300 by 12, 18 and 24 instead of 36 (they use only one of the denominators).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: If a/(b + c) = b/(c + a) = c/(a + b) = k, where the denominators are not zero, what are the possible values of k?

solution.concept: Add numerators and denominators of equal ratios, but watch the case a + b + c = 0
solution.explanation: If a + b + c ≠ 0, adding gives k = (a + b + c)/(2(a + b + c)) = ½. If a + b + c = 0, then b + c = −a, so k = a/(−a) = −1. Example: a = 1, b = 2, c = −3 gives each ratio −1.
steps: Case a + b + c ≠ 0: k = ½
Case a + b + c = 0: b + c = −a ⇒ k = −1
solution.why_others_wrong: ½ only misses the case a + b + c = 0 (for example 1, 2, −3); −1 only misses a = b = c; 2 inverts ½.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: An engine alone runs at 42 km/h. When it pulls wagons, its speed falls by an amount that varies as the square root of the number of wagons. With 9 wagons its speed is 24 km/h. What is the largest number of wagons it can pull and still move?

solution.concept: Fall in speed = k√n; the engine moves only while 42 − k√n > 0
solution.explanation: With 9 wagons the fall is 42 − 24 = 18 = k × 3, so k = 6. The engine moves while 6√n < 42, that is √n < 7, n < 49. The largest whole number of wagons is 48.
solution.why_others_wrong: With 49 wagons the speed is exactly 0, so it cannot move; 36 uses k = 7; 7 is the limit for √n, not n.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Riya was born when her mother was 27 years old. The sum of their present ages is 63 years. How old is Riya?

solution.concept: The mother is always 27 years older: mother = Riya + 27
solution.explanation: Riya + (Riya + 27) = 63, so 2 × Riya = 36 and Riya = 18. Her mother is 45.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 is the mother's age; 21 divides 63 by 3; 36 is 63 − 27, which is twice Riya's age.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Three years ago A was twice as old as B. Seven years from now A will be 1.5 times as old as B. What is the sum of their present ages?

solution.concept: Write both conditions in terms of the present ages a and b
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 is the sum three years ago; 50 is the sum seven years from now; 33 takes A as 20.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The ages of a grandfather and his grandson are in the ratio 15 : 2, and the grandfather is 65 years older. What will be the ratio of their ages 5 years from now?

solution.concept: The age gap of 65 years equals 15 − 2 = 13 parts
solution.explanation: 13 parts = 65, so 1 part = 5: grandfather 75, grandson 10. In 5 years: 80 and 15, ratio 16 : 3.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 : 2 is the present ratio; 17 : 4 is the ratio 10 years from now (85 : 20); 3 : 16 is inverted.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The product of the present ages of two brothers is 240. Four years ago the product of their ages was 132. How old is the elder brother?

solution.concept: Expand (a − 4)(b − 4) = ab − 4(a + b) + 16 to find the sum of the ages
solution.explanation: 240 − 4(a + b) + 16 = 132, so a + b = 31. Two numbers with sum 31 and product 240 are 16 and 15. The elder is 16.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 is the younger brother; 20 and 12 multiply to 240 but four years ago they give 16 × 8 = 128, not 132.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: What is the average of the first 25 odd numbers (1, 3, 5, …, 49)?

solution.concept: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n², so their average is n
solution.explanation: Sum = 25² = 625, and 625 ÷ 25 = 25. (Also: average = (first + last)/2 = (1 + 49)/2 = 25.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 26 takes the last number as 51; 24.5 averages 1 to 48; 50 adds the first and last numbers without halving.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The average age of a 7-member committee today is the same as it was 4 years ago, because one old member has been replaced by a younger one. How much younger is the new member than the member replaced?

solution.concept: In 4 years the total age of 7 people rises by 7 × 4 = 28; the replacement must cancel this
solution.explanation: Without the change the total would have grown by 28 years. For the average to stay the same, the new member must be 28 years younger than the member replaced.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 years is the time gap; 7 is the committee size; 32 adds the 4 years again.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The numbers 1, 2, 3, …, n are written on a board and one of them is erased. The average of the remaining numbers is 35 7/17. Which number was erased?

solution.concept: The average of the rest is close to n/2, and n − 1 must be a multiple of 17
solution.explanation: The average 602/17 needs n − 1 to be a multiple of 17, and n is about 2 × 35 = 70, so n − 1 = 68 and n = 69. Sum of 1 to 69 = 2,415. Remaining sum = 68 × 602/17 = 2,408, so the erased number is 2,415 − 2,408 = 7.
solution.why_others_wrong: Erasing 8, 17 or 35 leaves totals of 2,407, 2,398 or 2,380; only erasing 7 leaves 2,408.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A vendor buys bananas at 12 for ₹30 and sells them at 10 for ₹30. What is his profit percentage?

solution.concept: Compare the cost and the selling price of one banana
solution.explanation: Cost of one banana = 30 ÷ 12 = ₹2.50; selling price = 30 ÷ 10 = ₹3. Profit = ₹0.50 on ₹2.50 = 20%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16⅔% divides the profit by the selling price; 25% divides 0.50 by 2; 10% takes the gap of 2 bananas out of 20.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper marks a heater 30% above its cost price. Selling it at the marked price gives him a profit of ₹540. What is the cost price?

solution.concept: At the marked price the profit is the full 30% of the cost price
solution.explanation: 30% of CP = ₹540, so CP = 540 ÷ 0.3 = ₹1,800 (and the marked price is ₹2,340).
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹2,340 is the marked price; ₹1,260 takes ₹540 as 30% of the marked price; ₹2,160 is 1,800 × 1.2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A cloth seller's metre rod is 4 cm short. He sells cloth at 4% above the cost price per metre, measuring with this rod. What is his actual gain percentage?

solution.concept: He charges for 100 cm (at 1.04 × cost) but gives only 96 cm
solution.explanation: For each 'metre' he receives 1.04 × the cost of 100 cm while giving cloth costing 0.96 of that. Gain = 1.04 ÷ 0.96 − 1 = 1/12 = 8⅓%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8% simply adds 4% + 4%; 4% counts only the markup; 4⅙% counts only the short rod (4 ÷ 96).

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: Ravi buys a used phone and sells it at a 20% profit. Later he buys it back at 10% less than he sold it for, and then sells it again at a 10% profit on the buy-back price. What is his overall profit as a percentage of the original cost?

solution.concept: Track every rupee paid and received, starting from a cost of 100
solution.explanation: Cost 100. Sells for 120. Buys back for 90% of 120 = 108. Sells for 110% of 108 = 118.8. Net = −100 + 120 − 108 + 118.8 = 30.8, a profit of 30.8% on the original cost.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18.8% compares only the last sale with the original cost; 32% compounds 20% and 10%; 30% adds 20% and 10%.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: The profit made by selling an article for ₹1,260 is twice the loss made by selling it for ₹960. What is its cost price?

solution.why_others_wrong: ₹1,110 makes the profit equal to the loss; ₹1,160 makes the loss twice the profit; ₹1,080 gives a profit of 180 and a loss of 120.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A trader marks his goods x% above cost and then allows a discount of (x/2)% on the marked price, making a profit of 10.5%. If the markup is less than 50%, what is x?

solution.explanation: Try x = 30: 1.30 × 0.85 = 1.105 ✓. The equation x² − 100x + 2,100 = 0 has roots 30 and 70; since the markup is below 50%, x = 30.
solution.why_others_wrong: 70 also satisfies the equation but breaks the condition that the markup is below 50%; 21 doubles 10.5; 20 gives 1.2 × 0.9 = 1.08, only 8% profit.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.question_text: A grocer mixes 1 kg of stones into every 9 kg of lentils. He uses an 800 g weight in place of 1 kg and charges 8% above the cost price of lentils. What is his actual gain percentage?

solution.concept: The customer pays for 1 kg of lentils but receives 800 g of mixture, of which 90% is lentils
